newsitem.title: USA: American Home to cut debt with unit sale.
newsitem.headline: American Home to cut debt with unit sale.

text.p: American Home Products Corp's shedding of a business that sold popcorn and canned ravioli will help the company pay down debt while focusing it on its higher-margin healthcare divisions.

Analyst said American Home did well in selling 80 percent of its food products unit to private investment firm Hicks, Muse, Tate & Furst Inc for $1.2 billion in cash, while retaining the remaining stake.
"In general it's going to help them focus more on their pharmaceutical business and help them raise their gross margin," said Rodman & Renshaw analyst Mario Corso.

American Home's shares were up 1-1/8 to 60-1/8 in afternoon trading after the deal's announcement. The Madison, N.J.-based company had said in May that it was seeking buyers for the food unit that includes the Chef Boyardee, PAM cooking spray, Dennison's Chili and Jiffy Pop popcorn brands.
Cowen and Co analyst Ian Sanderson estimated the cash and 20 percent stake was worth about $1.5 billion to American Home, a price above his forecast of about $1.2 billion.
Hicks, Muse put the value of the deal at $1.3 billion.

"For (American Home) to sell a business that's probably growing at two-to-five percent over the next several years, they did very well," Sanderson said. He estimated the food business had a pretax profit margin of 11 percent, compared with margins of 18 to 22 percent for the rest of American Home's businesses, which include drugs such as Premarin hormone replacement therapy, medical devices, and consumer healthcare products including Advil pain reliever.
The food unit "was really just a laggard," Sanderson said.
Hicks, Muse said the food unit was expected to have sales of about $1.0 billion in 1996, up from $819 million in 1995 but in line with 1994's sales of $997 million.
American Home will use money from the sale to pay down debt and provide funds for "future strategic uses," a company spokesman said.
He said American Home, which paid $9.6 billion for its 1994 acquisition of American Cyanamid, had a gross debt of $7.4 billion and a goal to cut the debt to $5.0 billion by the end of 1997.
But American Home, with a relatively strong drug research and development pipeline, is not likely to race out and use the cash from the sale for a major acquisition, analysts said.

The company has said it has six new drugs it expects can generate over $500 million each in peak annual sales, including Rapamune for preventing organ rejection, a bone growth hormone factor and the Effexor line of anti-depressants.

"A year down the road maybe they'll have to reassess things, and if the pipeline projects haven't worked out, then they have to think about another big acquisition or something like that," Salomon Brothers analyst Robert Uhl said.

Analysts said the sale would likely have no impact on American Home's 1996 earnings. Sanderson said it could add $0.01 or $0.02 to its 1997 earnings, forecasted by Wall Street analysts at about $2.94 a share. It earned $2.39 a share in 1995, adjusted for a stock split and one-time items.
